description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.
proof_strategy: Define a phantom topology as a function T: O -> Top(X) from a set of observers to topologies on X. Define the intersection topology T_cap = intersection of all T(o). Prove: every second-countable T_0 space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with |O| = 2. Proof: for a basis {B_n}, define T(o1) as the topology generated by {B_n : n odd} union {X} and T(o2) by {B_n : n even} union {X}. Then T_cap = tau. Prove non-metrizable spaces need >= 3 observers: the Zariski topology on R^2 cannot be written as the intersection of two first-countable topologies. Test: verify the R example and construct the 3-observer phantom representation for the Zariski topology.
title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them

description: We conjecture that the finite Chromonic Lemma extends to infinite, locally finite, strongly connected digraphs. If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. The Color Blend Axiom ensures the limit respects blending, and strong connectivity yields a contradiction unless the coloring is constant. Alternatively, formulate the condition as a fixed‑point equation on the space of colorings and apply a Banach‑type contraction argument using the weights and the axiom.

description: We conjecture that the explicit bound $P^+(d)$ from the main theorem is optimal: for every $g\ge 2$, $d\in\{2g+1,2g+2\}$ and the corresponding $P^+(d)$, there exist a non‑zero algebraic integer $\alpha$ and a prime $p=P^+(d)$ (with $p\nmid N_{\mathbb Q(\alpha)/\mathbb Q}(\alpha)$) such that the family $\cC_\alpha\colon y^2 = x^d + \alpha x + t$ is **not** generically ordinary at $p$. In other words, the threshold $p>P^+(d)$ cannot be lowered.
proof_strategy: 1. Use the explicit counterexamples constructed by Katz (e.g. $(d,p)=(21,359)$, $(31,839)$, $(51,2399)$) together with a suitable choice of $\alpha$ (take $\alpha=-d$ for the original Katz family) to verify directly that the Hasse‑Witt matrix of the reduction $\cC_\alpha$ modulo $p$ has determinant zero for $p=P^+(d)$. 2. Generalise these computations to arbitrary $d$ by showing that the vanishing pattern of the Hasse‑Witt matrix persists for any $\alpha$ with $p\nmid N_{\mathbb Q(\alpha)/\mathbb Q}(\alpha)$, using the known description of the Cartier‑Manin matrix for hyperelliptic curves in terms of the polynomial $x^d+\alpha x+t$. 3. Conclude that the bound $P^+(d)$ is best possible; any lower bound would be contradicted by these explicit families.
title: Sharpness of the ordinary bound for hyperelliptic families

description: We conjecture that for any two independent sets I and I' in a P4-tidy graph G, a token sliding reconfiguration of I into I' exists if and only if they share the same cardinality and every induced P4 in G has a vertex in I ∩ I' or is resolved by a vertex not in I ∪ I'. This condition ensures that reconfiguration can proceed through local sliding moves without creating forbidden induced P4 structures.
proof_strategy: Demonstrate via graph decomposition that P4-tidy graphs can be partitioned into clique-forest-like components connected through controlled bipartite interfaces, enabling step-by-step reconfiguration while maintaining invariants at P4-critical vertices.
title: Reconfigurable Independent Sets in P4-Tidy Graphs via Token Sliding

description: Let ℓ be a fixed prime and let 𝔽 be a non‑isotrivial one‑parameter family of abelian varieties over ℚ such that the ℓ‑torsion Galois module A[ℓ] is constant (i.e. isomorphic to a fixed finite 𝔽_ℓ‑module M for every fibre). For each rational prime p of good reduction for the specialised fibre A_t, the Greenberg–Wiles formula gives a local factor c_p(A_t)∈ℕ that yields the inequality |Sel_ℓ(A_t)| ≥ c_p(A_t). The conjecture asserts that for 100 % of primes p (ordered by size) the inequality is an equality, i.e. the global ℓ‑Selmer size is exactly the product of the local lower bounds predicted by Greenberg–Wiles.
proof_strategy: Define in Lean the Greenberg–Wiles local factor c_p(A) using the ramification‑measuring maps 𝔅_p and 𝔏_p from the paper. Prove that for a constant‑torsion family the global ℓ‑Selmer group decomposes as the restricted product of the local cohomology groups with the prescribed local conditions, so its order equals the product of the orders of the local quotients H¹(G_p,M)/H¹_𝔏(p)(G_p,M). Show that for almost all primes the unramified subgroup H¹_ur(G_p,M) is maximal among admissible local conditions, which forces the inequality to be an equality. Use Chebotarev density to argue that the set of primes where extra ramification could increase the Selmer size has density zero. Formalise the density argument via Dirichlet density in Lean, and combine with the explicit description of the Greenberg–Wiles pairing Ω_𝔏 to obtain the desired equality for density‑one set of primes.
title: Sharpness of the Greenberg–Wiles local lower bound for ℓ‑Selmer groups in constant‑torsion families

description: Conjecture that a torsion Hecke eigenclass in the cohomology of the arithmetic manifold attached to GL_n over a CM number field F with coefficients in Z/ℓ^m gives rise to a continuous semisimple Galois representation r : G_F → GL_n(Z_ℓ) which is de Rham at places v|ℓ, with Hodge–Tate weights determined by the infinitesimal character of the automorphic representation at infinity, and whose associated filtered φ‑module via Fontaine's functor corresponds under the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence to the automorphic component π_v.

title: Torsion local-global compatibility at p = ℓ for GL_n over CM fields

description:
Conjecture: For any fixed integer r≥2 and any collection of graphs H1, …, Hr, let ψ = ∥_{j=1}^r (ω67(Hj)‑1). Define the critical edge density π_c = 1‑1/ψ. For a host graph G0 on n vertices with edge density exactly π_c−ε (for a fixed ε>0) consider the random‑perturbation model where we add m random edges (without replacement). Then the minimal number of edges that forces the perturbed graph to be (H1, …, Hr)_v‑Ramsey satisfies

    m_c(n) = π_c * (n choose 2) + Ψ(n^{3/2}),

and there is a sharp threshold: if m = m_c(n) + ω(n^{3/2}) then with high probability the perturbed graph is (H1, …, Hr)_v‑Ramsey; if m = m_c(n) − ω(n^{3/2}) then with high probability it is not. Moreover, the window of size O(n^{3/2}) is the critical window for the transition.
proof_strategy: 1. Prove a stability theorem characterising vertex‑Ramsey graphs as Turán‑type graphs with only a few missing edges. 2. Derive supersaturation results for the vertex‑Ramsey property in terms of edge density. 3. Apply differential‑equation / sparse random graph techniques to the random‑edge addition process, establishing that once the density exceeds π_c by ≈ n^{−1/2} the property holds w.h.p., and that below this threshold it fails w.h.p. via a second‑moment or Chernoff argument. 4. Combine these to locate the critical window of width θ(n^{3/2}).
title: Precise threshold for vertex‑Ramsey property in random perturbations

description: The sheared Witt vector functor preserves filtered colimits over nilperfect rings. Specifically, for any filtered category I and diagram (R_i)_{i ∈ I} of nilperfect rings, the canonical morphism chW(\varinjlim R_i) → \varinjlim chW(R_i) is an isomorphism. This property is the key motivation for the sheared Witt construction and resolves the obstruction in extending Dieudonné theory to non-perfect rings.
proof_strategy: The conjecture follows from verifying that the pullback defining chW(R) commutes with filtered colimits. Key steps: (1) Show hw(\varinjlim R_i) ≅ \varinjlim hw(R_i) for the ideal hw(R), (2) Prove \varprojlim_F W(R)/hw(R) commutes with filtered colimits, and (3) Use the pullback compatibility with filtered limits. The nilperfect condition ensures the Frobenius inverse system behaves well under colimits.
title: Filtered Colimit Preservation by Sheared Witt Vectors

title: Combinatorial Interpretation of $s$-Rook Polynomials via $(p,q)$-Deformed Normal Ordering

description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
proof_strategy: Define an Escher staircase in ring R as a strictly ascending chain I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... such that intersection of I_n is contained in I_1. Prove Int(Z) has an Escher staircase: I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z}. Each I_n is strictly contained in I_{n+1} (the polynomial x choose n is in I_{n+1} but not I_n). Intersection of I_n = {0} contained in I_1. Prove k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n: the chain (x_1) contained in (x_1,x_2) contained in ... contained in (x_1,...,x_n) has length n. Prove Z_p has no Escher staircase (Noetherian). Test: verify for Int(Z) and k[x,y,z].
title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back

This conjecture refines the already verified AVD‑TCC bound for central graphs of regular graphs and predicts exact values.

This yields $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) \ge d+3$. 2. **Upper bound**: Build an explicit AVD‑total coloring of $C(G)$ with $d+3$ colors. The coloring proceeds by first coloring the original vertices of $G$ with $d+1$ colors respecting regularity, then extending to the subdivision vertices and the added universal edges in such a way that adjacent vertex colour‑sets remain distinct. The construction uses known colourings for regular graphs and the fact that $C(G)$ is obtained from $S(G)$ by joining non‑adjacent vertices, which simplifies the constraints. Combining both directions gives the desired equality (or the exceptional value for $K_{d+1}$).
title: Exact AVD‑total chromatic number of central graphs of regular graphs

description: Let Φ be any irreducible root system and H_aff the associated affine Hecke algebra over ℤ[v^±1]. The subalgebra 𝔅_aff⊂H_aff introduced as a pseudo‑centralizer in the double affine Hecke algebra admits a canonical basis {b_w清} indexed by the cosets w∈W_aff/W_fin. The conjecture states that for all w₁,w₂∈W_aff/W_fin the product expands as b_{w₁}⋅b_{w₂}=∑_{w₃}c_{w₁,w₂}^{w₃}b_{w₃} with each coefficient c_{w₁,w₂}^{w₃}∈ℕ[v,v^{-1}], i.e. a polynomial with non‑negative integer coefficients. In particular, specializing v↦1 yields nonnegative integers. This is falsifiable by exhibiting a counterexample in any type.
proof_strategy: Use the combinatorial model for the affine Grassmannian homology given by Lam’s subalgebra and the explicit description of 𝔅_aff in types A_n, B_2, G_2. Show that the canonical basis coincides with the dual canonical basis of the associated quantum group, for which positivity of structure constants is known. Employ induction on the length of affine Weyl group elements, braid relations, and the positivity of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. Verify the conjecture in low rank types by computer algebra (Sage/Lean) to support the pattern, then generalize using the categorification via Soergel bimodules.
title: Positivity of structure constants for the canonical basis of 𝔅_aff

description: We conjecture that the Chromatic Sum problem exhibits a complexity dichotomy based on the structure of the forbidden graph H: it is polynomial-time solvable on H-free graphs when H is a forest, and NP-complete when H contains at least one cycle. This directly extends the complete classification mentioned in the paper for H-free graphs.
proof_strategy: 1) Prove membership in P for forest H by constructing an algorithm leveraging the structural properties of H-free graphs (e.g., bounded clique-width or decomposition techniques). 2) Prove NP-hardness for non-forest H by adapting the reduction techniques from planar subcubic graphs and bounded independence number frameworks in the paper. 3) Formalize both directions using graph minors, tree-width, and forbidden subgraph machinery in Lean 4.
title: Chromatic Sum Complexity Dichotomy for Forest-Forbidden Graphs

description: Formulate a statement asserting that for a self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\Pi_0$ of $\text{PGL}_3(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$, the proportion of zeros of the twisted $L$-function $L(s, \Pi_0 \times \chi)$ lying on the critical line $\text{Re}(s) = 1/2$ is at least $1/9$ as the conductor $Q$ of the Dirichlet character $\chi$ tends to infinity.
proof_strategy: The proof requires formalizing the theory of automorphic $L$-functions for $\text{GL}_3$, the Dirichlet-series-based mollification method, and Levinson's method for zero-detection. One would need to define the density of zeros using the argument principle and show that the mollified mean value of the $L$-function derivative satisfies specific asymptotic inequalities that force zeros onto the line $\sigma = 1/2$.
title: Lower Bound for the Proportion of Zeros on the Critical Line for PGL(3) L-functions

description: This conjecture predicts that under the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, the dimension of the Selmer group over a finite number field $K$ of conductor $N$ grows asymptotically as a function of the Euler characteristic of the stabilizer, mirroring the fan structure described in the paper. It provides a falsifiable benchmark for the number of Selmer ranks attained by a fixed elliptic curve in cyclic extensions.
proof_strategy: Construct a probabilistic model inspired by the fan structure and apply ergodic arguments under mild GT conditions.
title: Fan-structured order and uniform bounds in the Selmer group distribution

description: In the setting of the paper, let K be a subcomplex of the join of all spanning k‑trees of a complete (k+1)-partite graph on disjoint finite vertex sets V₁,…,V_{k+1} together with a wedge of an m‑sphere. Conjecture: Every colorful Carathéodory map A:|K|→ℝ^{k+1} must contain a non‑empty face of dimension at most k that maps to 0, and the collection of such minimal faces forms exactly the flag complex of the hypergraph of spanning k‑trees satisfying a certain exchange property. This conjecture is falsifiable: for specific choices of k, d and wedge dimension one can construct a counterexample if the claimed bound on dimension is violated.
proof_strategy: Induction on k combined with parity arguments analogous to Meshulam's lemma
title: Conjecture on minimal hitting subcomplexes in joins of spanning k‑trees with wedge of spheres

description: For any s ∈ ℕ₀, h ∈ ℂ\{0}, and non-negative integers n,k, the (p,q)-generalized Stirling numbers 𝔖_{s;h}(n,k|p,q) defined by the normal ordering of (YX)^n in the (p,q)-deformed generalized Weyl algebra can be expressed as a linear combination of (p,q)-binomial coefficients with non-negative integer coefficients.
proof_strategy: Use the combinatorial interpretation via (p,q)-deformed s-rook placements on staircase boards to construct an explicit bijection between rook placements and the terms in the (p,q)-binomial expansion, showing that each rook placement contributes positively.
title: Positivity of (p,q)-Generalized Stirling Numbers in the (p,q)-Binomial Basis

description: Formalize the upper bound on the maximum size of a Sidon subset of {0, ..., N-1}, specifically proving that F(N) <= N^{1/2} + 0.94601 * N^{1/4} + O(1), by implementing the vector-valued convolution inequality and the rational certificate for the constant gamma_0.
proof_strategy: 1. Define the property of being a Sidon set in Lean 4. 2. Implement the vector-valued smoothing lemma, defining a weighted Hilbert direct sum of smoothing kernels. 3. Formalize the analytic reduction from the Sidon property to a convolution inequality involving these kernels. 4. Encode the provided rational certificate as a set of explicit rational coefficients and verify the boundary majorant condition via the provided exact arithmetic logic. 5. Use the resulting constant gamma_0 to derive the asymptotic upper bound on F(N).
title: Upper Bound for the Cardinality of Finite Sidon Sets

catalog_references: Niessen's result on at most three overfull subgraphs
description: Every class 2 graph G with Δ(G) > |V(G)|/3 contains an induced Δ(G)-overfull subgraph H such that every vertex in V(G)\V(H) has degree at most Δ(G) - 2 in the original graph G. This conjecture strengthens the Overfull Conjecture by asserting not just existence but also a structural property: the overfull subgraph can be found so that removing it reduces the maximum degree significantly.
proof_strategy: Approach by contradiction assuming no such subgraph exists. Use Edmonds' matching theory to derive constraints on the matching structure. Apply discharging arguments based on the high-degree vertices outside V(H). Leverage the known result that at most three overfull subgraphs exist (Niessen 2001) to bound the structure. Analyze the Petersen graph P* as the critical threshold case to understand extremal configurations.
title: Structural Location of Overfull Subgraphs in Class 2 Graphs

catalog_references: Cameron, Ellis & Raynaud, *Cyclically covering subspaces over finite fields*, 2019

description: For any odd prime power q≥3 and integer m≥4, the largest codimension of a cyclically covering subspace of 𝔽_qⁿ with n=(q^m+1)/2 equals 1. Equivalently, there exists a cyclic code of length (q^m+1)/2 and dimension n−1 that contains no full‑weight codeword, and no cyclically covering subspace of larger codimension can exist.
domain_bridges: finite geometry (covering radius of dual codes)
proof_strategy: Construct an explicit cyclic code of length n=(q^m+1)/2 whose generator polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a primitive element of 𝔽_{q^m} of order q^m+1 divided by (x−1). Show that this code has dimension n−1 and that every nonzero codeword has at least one zero coordinate (hence no full‑weight codeword). Using the characterization h_q(n)=0 iff every nonzero cyclic code contains a full‑weight codeword, deduce h_q(n)>0; then prove that any larger codimension would force the existence of a full‑weight codeword, contradicting the structure of the cyclotomic cosets for length n. This establishes h_q(n)=1. The proof relies on finite–field trace maps, cyclotomic coset enumeration, and the covering property equivalence established in the cited works.
title: Exact Codimension for Cyclically Covering Subspaces of Length (qᵐ+1)/2

description: For a family of unitary CFTs dual to AdS black holes with central charge c → ∞, let M_c denote the maximal number of primary operators in a fixed energy window of width Δ. Define the centered and scaled variable Y_c = (log M_c - μ_c)/σ_c, where μ_c and σ_c are the mean and standard deviation of log M_c. Conjecture that Y_c converges in distribution to the Gumbel law, i.e., for every real x, \(\lim_{c\to\infty} P(Y_c \leq x) = \exp(-\exp(-x))\).
proof_strategy: Leverage known results on the convergence of extremal statistics of Gaussian log‑correlated processes to the Gumbel distribution, combine them with a rigorous saddle‑point analysis of the CFT partition function to identify the appropriate scaling of μ_c and σ_c, and verify the required tightness and moment conditions for the limit theorem.
title: Gumbel limit for extremal microstate counts in AdS/CFT

proof_strategy: Prove the equivalence by constructing an explicit finite subcover from a minimal sequence and using the universal property of the direct sum to relate induced homomorphisms to sums of ψ_i.
title: Kernel‑cover characterisation of the weighted Davenport constant

description: Conjecture: Let A be a line arrangement in the complex projective plane of degree d such that every singular point has multiplicity at most 3 (i.e., only double and triple points). If the minimal degree of a Jacobian relation satisfies mdr(A) < d/2, then mdr(A) is combinatorially determined: any other line arrangement B with the same intersection lattice (and hence the same singularity multiplicities) has mdr(B) = mdr(A).
proof_strategy: Use the fact that for arrangements with only double and triple points the Jacobian ideal is generated by the partial derivatives of a defining polynomial that is known to be quasi-homogeneous with respect to certain weights. Apply Saito's criterion for freeness and the relation between the exponents of the arrangement and the degrees of minimal syzygies. Show that under the hypothesis mdr < d/2 the arrangement is plus-one generated, which forces the Jacobian syzygy module to have a predictable graded structure determined solely by the intersection lattice. Verify the claim by computing the relevant graded Betti numbers via Gröbner basis techniques in the polynomial ring S = C[x,y,z].
title: Combinatorial determination of mdr for line arrangements with only double and triple points

title: Geodesic Treewidth Upper Bound for Planar Graphs

description: We conjecture that for any oriented product structure \((A,B,P)\) of type \((m,n)\) with \(m,n\ge2\) satisfying the no‑fold condition \(\mathsf T_2\), the weighted dual Fisher inequality is strict unless \((m,n)=(2,2)\) and the structure is the affine plane of order 2 (i.e. the unique 2×2 grid). Moreover, if the middle‑link girth is 6 then the minimum of the two horizontal‑link girths is at most 4, and equality in the weighted dual Fisher inequality forces the structure to be exactly this affine‑plane construction. This would classify all extremal cases of the combinatorial inequalities underlying the taiko assembly theorem.
proof_strategy: We would formalize the definition of an oriented product structure, its girth functions, the no‑fold condition, and the weighted dual Fisher inequality in Lean. Then we would perform a computer‑assisted search over all product structures with support sizes up to a reasonable bound (e.g. \(m,n\le 10\)). For each candidate we check the inequality; any case attaining equality is recorded. Using combinatorial reasoning (product identity, pressure inequalities, Fisher bounds) we would then prove that any equality case must have \(m=n=2\) and be isomorphic to the 2×2 affine plane. The search provides falsifying examples if the conjecture is false, while the reasoning supplies a proof of the classification.
title: Equality case of the weighted dual Fisher inequality for taiko product structures

description: For a Hamiltonian graph G with minimum degree at least 3, there exists a constant c > 0 such that G contains a nontrivial cycle of length at least n - c n^{2/3}. The proof combines a constructive method using a poset-based edge-disjoint cycle decomposition with a nonconstructive application of the probabilistic method, leveraging the best possible bounds achievable via these approaches.
proof_strategy: Establish that all long cycles are blocked by a specific edge, then use a cycle-pairing strategy from poset theory to construct a nontrivial cycle, augmented by a probabilistic counting argument to ensure the existence of a sufficiently long alternative cycle.
title: Existence of a nontrivial cycle of length n-O(n^{2/3}) in Hamiltonian graphs with δ(G) ≥ 3

description: We conjecture that for every λ > 1 with gcd(λ,6) = 1, the λ‑skeleton L_λ contains infinitely many rows that contain at least one prime. Equivalently, the set of prime‑free rows in L_λ is finite. This extends the paper's result that only the principal skeleton L_1 has the infinite prime‑free arithmetic progression k ≡ 2 (mod 4).
proof_strategy:
1. Formalize the predicate in Lean and perform exhaustive searches for small λ (e.g., λ = 5,7,11,…) to collect many examples of primes in rows, establishing empirical evidence.

2. Use known results on primes in exponential sequences (e.g., the Bunyakovsky conjecture applied to the polynomial λ·2^a·3^b – 1) together with sieve methods to argue infinitude for each fixed λ.

3. Apply Zsigmondy’s theorem to guarantee new prime divisors in terms of a,b, which can be used to deduce the existence of primes in infinitely many rows.

4. Attempt a formal proof in Lean using the mathlib prime number theory lemmas and induction on k to show that for any λ>1, beyond a certain bound all rows contain a prime.
title: Infinite prime rows in λ‑skeletons beyond λ=1

catalog_references: Spherical Designs with Infinite Harmonic Strength
description: For any finite antipodal set X on the d-dimensional sphere (d ≥ 2), if the harmonic strength Hst(X) contains any even integer, then it must contain 2. This would imply that the smallest even degree in the harmonic strength of an antipodal design is always 2.
proof_strategy: Investigate the relationship between the moment tensors of antipodal sets. For an antipodal set X, the sum of harmonic polynomials of degree 2k is related to the 2k-th moment tensor. If all odd moments vanish (by antipodality), the condition for degree 2 to be in Hst(X) is that the inertia tensor is proportional to the identity. If degree 2 is not in Hst(X), the inertia tensor has distinct eigenvalues. Use representation theory of O(d+1) to show that if a higher even moment vanishes, then the inertia tensor must be isotropic, forcing degree 2 to vanish. Alternatively, construct a counterexample by finding an antipodal set with Hst(X) containing 4 but not 2.
title: Even Harmonic Strength of Antipodal Spherical Designs Contains 2

Use the Lindström-Gessel-Viennot (LGV) lemma or a similar combinatorial path-counting method to show that the determinants of all minors are non-negative, leveraging the combinatorial proof provided in the paper.
title: Total Positivity of the Interval Subdivision Transformation Matrix

Use induction on N and properties of the counting function C(·,·).

catalog_references: On the Linearity of Squarefree Powers of Edge Ideals (arXiv:2204.12345)
description: For a 1-dimensional flag simplicial complex $\Delta$ and its Stanley-Reisner ideal $I_\Delta$, the squarefree power $I_\Delta^{[p]}$ has a linear resolution if and only if the Krull dimension of $S/I_\Delta^{[p]}$ equals $2p$. This conjecture formalizes the combinatorial characterization provided in the paper by linking the algebraic property of linear resolutions to a dimension-theoretic condition.
proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by analyzing the structure of $\Delta^{[p]}$ (the Stanley-Reisner complex of $I_\Delta^{[p]}$) and its facets. When $\dim S/I_\Delta^{[p]} = 2p$, the absence of high-dimensional obstructions ensures the first syzygies are generated by linear forms. Conversely, when $\dim S/I_\Delta^{[p]} = 2p-1$, the ideal coincides with a squarefree Veronese ideal whose non-Cohen-Macaulayness (when $n < 2d$) prevents a linear resolution. The proof would require verifying that the combinatorial characterization of $\Delta^{[p]}$ facets matches the dimension criterion.
title: Linear Resolution Criterion for Squarefree Powers of Stanley-Reisner Ideals

description:

Thus, apart from the three small exceptions, the property "all b‑invariant edges are forcing" precisely picks out the near‑bipartite bricks.

This uses the structural lemmas from the paper (e.g. that b‑invariant edges in such bricks are exactly the subdivided edges of the perfect matching).
   - (≃) Assuming every b‑invariant edge is forcing, deduce that G cannot contain a non‑ne
title: Every b‑invariant edge is forcing exactly for near‑bipartite bricks (up to the three classical exceptions)

proof_strategy: Construct H(P) explicitly and verify tree properties via induction on the equivalence classes of chains.
title: H(P) is a tree under the domination order for countable FAC posets avoiding specified saturated chains

description: Conjecture that for any rational polytopal measure P in ℝ^d, the set of hyperplanes that bisect P is exactly the real zero set of a finite system of polynomial equations with rational coefficients derived from the coordinates of the defining polytopes; moreover, this system can be effectively computed and each solution corresponds to an algebraic number of bounded degree.
proof_strategy: Show that the bisecting condition translates to polynomial equations via the cap-volume function; apply quantifier elimination to obtain a semialgebraic description; verify that the resulting variety matches the set of bisecting hyperplanes.
title: Semialgebraic Characterization of Bisecting Hyperplanes for Rational Polytopal Measures

description: Deja vu — the feeling that you've experienced something before — is a fixed point in a dynamical system. Model cognitive state as a function f: S -> S mapping current brain state to next brain state. A deja vu is a state s such that f^n(s) = s for some n > 0 — a periodic point of the cognitive dynamical system. Conjecture: By Sharkovsky's theorem, the existence of a period-3 orbit in the cognitive dynamics (three distinct states that cycle) implies chaos in the sense of Li-Yorke, meaning there exist uncountably many cognitive trajectories that are neither periodic nor convergent. Moreover, the set of deja vu states (periodic points of f) is dense in the cognitive state space S if f is continuous and S is an interval. The frequency of deja vu (occurring in ~70% of people) corresponds to the natural density of periodic points in a typical chaotic map. Test: model cognitive dynamics as a logistic map f(x) = rx(1-x) on [0,1] with parameter r chosen to match empirical deja vu frequencies. For r = 3.83 (period-3 window), compute the density of periodic points and compare to the 70% lifetime incidence. Impact: deja vu is not a glitch — it's a mathematical inevitability of continuous cognitive dynamics. Any continuous cognitive map with a period-3 orbit MUST have deja vu.
proof_strategy: Model cognitive state space as S = [0,1] and cognitive dynamics as f: S -> S continuous. Apply Sharkovsky's theorem: if f has a point of period 3, then f has points of all periods. A deja vu state is a periodic point: s such that f^n(s) = s. Prove: the set of periodic points is dense in S for the logistic map at r = 3.83. Compute the density of periodic points: PeriodicPoints_n(f) / n approaches the topological entropy h(f) as n -> infinity. For the logistic map at r = 3.83, h(f) ~ 0.38. The lifetime incidence of deja vu (~70%) is consistent with the probability that a random orbit encounters a periodic point neighborhood within a typical observation window. Test: simulate 10000 random orbits of the logistic map and count how many encounter periodic neighborhoods.
title: The Mathematics of Deja Vu: Fixed Points in Consciousness and Cognition

description:
# Future Directions — Congruence Rigidity of Sums of Squares

This cycle established that the entries of an integer right triangle are forced into
strong divisibility patterns — one leg is a multiple of three, the legs jointly carry a
factor of four, one entry is a multiple of five — and that a four-dimensional right
"box" (a solution of `a² + b² + c² = d²`) is even more rigid: at most one of its three
spatial edges can be odd. We also pinned down exactly which whole numbers can serve as a
leg. These findings point to several bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. The correct modulus for a power of two grows with the power
**Conjecture.** In any solution of `a² + b² = c²`, the two-adic valuation of the leg
product `a·b` is governed one level deeper than naive reduction suggests: deciding
whether `2^k` divides `a·b` is a question about residues modulo `2^{k+1}`, never modulo
`2^k`.
*The key insight is* that a difference of two odd squares is always divisible by eight,
so each additional factor of two in the product must be certified one binary place
further out than one would guess. *Why now?* Having isolated the exact `mod 8`
obstruction behind the factor of four, we can test the pattern mechanically for `k = 3,
4, 5` and either confirm a clean "shift-by-one" law or expose its first exception.

## 2. A universal super-divisor for higher-dimensional right figures
**Conjecture.** For every dimension `r`, solutions of `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` obey a single
universal divisibility law: there is a constant `D(r)`, depending only on `r`, such that
`D(r)` divides the product `x₁·x₂·⋯·x_r` for *every* solution, and `D(r)` is the largest
such constant.
*The key insight is* that reduction to a finite residue ring turns "for all solutions"
into a finite, decidable statement, so the optimal constant `D(r)` is computable and
should grow in a structured (conjecturally multiplicative-over-primes) way. *Why now?*
The three-dimensional case already yields `4 ∣ x₁x₂x₃`; comparing it against the planar
constant `12` suggests a dimension-indexed sequence worth charting and predicting.

## 3. Parity collapse in higher dimensions
**Conjecture.** As the number of squared terms increases, the number of edges permitted to
be odd stays uniformly bounded: in `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` at most three of the `x_i` can be
odd, regardless of `r`.
*The key insight is* that the sum of squares equals the count of odd terms modulo four,
while a perfect square is `0` or `1` modulo four, capping the admissible odd-count no
matter how many terms are added. *Why now?* We proved the cap is "at most one" in three
dimensions; extending the modular bookkeeping to arbitrary `r` is a self-contained next
step that would reveal whether the cap is truly dimension-independent.

## 4. A sharp threshold characterization of legs in every dimension
**Conjecture.** Just as the whole numbers that are a leg of a right triangle are exactly
those `≥ 3`, in each higher dimension there is a sharp finite threshold above which every
integer appears as an edge of some right figure, and the finitely many exceptions can be
listed explicitly.
*The key insight is* that a single explicit construction, split according to the parity of
the target edge, realizes all sufficiently large values, while the small exceptions are
forced by a factorization that would otherwise require a vanishing edge. *Why now?* The
planar threshold `3` and its sharpness (the failures at `1` and `2`) give a template that
should transfer verbatim to the box equation and beyond.

## 5. Divisibility as a sieve against near-solutions
**Conjecture.** The combined congruence obstructions (`12 ∣ a·b`, `60 ∣ a·b·c`, and their
higher-dimensional analogues) are strong enough that a random integer triple satisfying
them has a positive, computable probability of being genuinely Pythagorean — i.e. the
congruence conditions capture a constant fraction of the "arithmetic mass" of true
solutions.
*The key insight is* that each universal divisor removes a fixed proportion of impostors,
so stacking independent prime-power obstructions multiplies into a sieve of predictable
density. *Why now?* With the exact obstructions in hand for the primes `2, 3, 5`, one can
immediately measure how much of the solution set they explain and calibrate whether a few
more primes suffice to pin down solutions almost completely.
title: That the entries of an integer right triangle are forced

description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
proof_strategy: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.
title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities

description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ... (each term avoids being the sum of the two previous terms). Conjecture: The anti-Fibonacci sequence A(n) grows as A(n) ~ n^2/4, and the ratio A(n)/n^2 converges to 1/4. More precisely, A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1). The sequence avoids the golden ratio entirely — the ratio A(n+1)/A(n) does NOT converge, instead oscillating between 1 and 2. The complement of the anti-Fibonacci sequence (numbers that ARE sums of two previous anti-Fibonacci numbers) has density 0. Test: compute A(n) for n up to 10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 approaches 1/4. Prove A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1) by induction. Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.
proof_strategy: Define A(1) = A(2) = 1, A(n+1) = smallest positive integer not equal to A(n) + A(n-1). Prove by strong induction: A(n) >= floor(n^2/4). Base: A(1)=1 >= 0, A(2)=1 >= 1. Inductive step: if A(k) >= floor(k^2/4) for k <= n, then A(n) + A(n-1) >= floor(n^2/4) + floor((n-1)^2/4), so A(n+1) <= A(n) + A(n-1) - 1 + delta where delta accounts for gaps, giving A(n+1) >= floor((n+1)^2/4). Prove A(n) <= ceil(n^2/4) + 1 by showing the avoidance constraint only blocks one value per step. Test: compute A(n) for n=1..10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 -> 1/4.
title: The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: Numbers That Avoid the Golden Ratio at All Costs
